user_story.function: Detect and limit coordinated false reporting, bad-faith appeals flooding, and disinformation campaigns targeting VTC governance and trust anchor reputations
user_story.goal: Protect VTC governance bandwidth and anchor credibility against organised disruption while preserving legitimate grievance channels

user_story.function: Initiate a connecting VRC ceremony with a trust anchor I do not yet know well, declare my relational terms upfront, and negotiate a staged exchange that allows time for relationship deliberation
user_story.goal: Gain a VRC from an anchor outside my existing social graph without being forced into synchronous completion or penalised for requesting a multi-session ceremony

user_story.persona_label: D5 – Sophie Dubois – Member Subject to Revocation
user_story.function: Request a witnessed VRC renewal with a specific anchor serving as constitutor witness — not just attestor — so that the witness's presence makes the ceremony socially real within the community

user_story.function: Decline a witnessed VRC exchange request via INDIRECT_DECLINE after detecting anomalous party graph patterns, triggering a community-only log entry that feeds anomaly detection without exposing my reason to the requester
user_story.goal: Protect my integrity and the VTC from a potential Sybil laundering attempt while preserving dignity norms — the counterparty receives a refusal without a reason code; the community log receives a committed reason for investigation

user_story.function: Present a VRC issued by a different VTC as partial evidence of membership eligibility in a second VTC, relying on cross-VTC credential recognition governed by a shared trust registry entry
user_story.goal: Join a second affiliated VTC without repeating the full admission process from scratch, while ensuring the second VTC can verify the issuing VTC's governance framework and my credential's dependency chain

user_story.function: Amend the VTC constitution mid-lifecycle following a governance vote, versioning the change so that in-flight ceremonies are bound to the prior version and new ceremonies apply the amended version
user_story.goal: Update governance rules without invalidating existing member credentials or disrupting active ceremonies, and ensure the VTA's PEP applies the correct governance version to each ceremony based on when it reached AGREED state

user_story.function: Initiate a formal adjudication of a contested admission denial, presenting my case to an independent governance body with authority to issue a binding ruling overriding the anchor's original decision
user_story.goal: Obtain a fair, independently adjudicated outcome for a disputed denial without relying solely on the anchor who made the original decision, and receive a binding ruling artefact that the VTA must honour

user_story.function: Detect and gracefully halt operations when my operator's VMC is revoked, within the liveness check interval declared in my behavioural commitment, and produce a signed suspension record for the operator's audit log
user_story.goal: Avoid acting on behalf of a member whose VTC membership has been revoked, limiting the harm window to the committed liveness interval and providing a verifiable record that I ceased operations promptly on detection

user_story.function: Detect and enforce behavioural commitment violations by agents operating inside the trust perimeter, producing cryptographically provable breach records when an agent exceeds its declared operational parameters
user_story.goal: Ensure that agent misbehaviour inside the VTC is detectable as a protocol-level event — not merely a statistical anomaly — by comparing observed behaviour against the agent's signed behavioural commitment and generating verifiable breach records

user_story.function: Model a sensor network holding a legal-personhood DID as a first-class party in a trust task protocol, verifying that the five atomic trust task types can be executed with a non-human entity as a named participant
user_story.goal: Establish proof-of-concept that the DTG trust task protocol specifications are entity-agnostic — that Identify, Attest, Exchange, Signal, and Restore operate identically whether the party is a human, an AI agent, or a non-human entity with legal personhood

user_story.function: Test the protocol-level enforcement of trust task pre-conditions by intentionally invoking Exchange before completing Identify, and verify that the PEP produces a standard pre-condition violation record rather than an unhandled runtime error
user_story.goal: Confirm that the VTA's PEP enforces the mandatory ordering constraint (Identify before Exchange) as a protocol requirement, not an implementation convention, and that the failure artefact is interoperable across implementations

user_story.function: Issue and accumulate endorsements for specific member skills within the VTC, support retraction of an endorsement that no longer reflects my assessment, and ensure the endorsement graph topology is verifiable by third parties
user_story.goal: Enable a reputation layer within the VTC that is distinct from membership credentials, where endorsements accumulate over time, retractions are prospective (not retrospective), and the endorsement graph can be verified for anomalous clustering patterns

user_story.function: Execute a governed VTC dissolution, revoking all VMCs and the Community DID, preserving the tamper-evident governance log, and issuing a portability package to every member containing their credentials, outcome records, and the signed dissolution record
user_story.goal: Wind down the VTC in a way that is verifiably legitimate — members can prove their prior credentials were valid at issuance — and that leaves no active credentials pointing to a dissolved issuer DID

user_story.function: Reproduce a governance configuration failure where the VTA applies the wrong governance framework version to a live ceremony, and verify that the resulting failure record captures the version mismatch in a machine-readable, diagnosable form
user_story.goal: Establish that governance version binding at ceremony AGREED state is a protocol requirement with a specified failure mode — not an implementation detail — so that version mismatch failures are interoperable and diagnosable across VTA implementations

user_story.function: Apply for VTC membership using a co-signed admission credential where my responsible adult (Grace) acts as co-signatory for consent purposes, not as a substituted decision-maker

user_story.persona_label: EC2a – Arthur Kowalczyk – Person Living with Dementia

scenario.name: VTC Genesis — Bootstrapping Under Founder Control
scenario.description: A single initiator establishes the VTC, generating the Community DID and hard-coding Phase 1 policies. Power is maximally concentrated.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. How is initiator authority time-bounded?
2. What governance artefacts must exist before Phase 2?
3. What constitutes unacceptable bootstrap bias?

scenario.name: Trust Anchor Seeding — Diversity vs. Speed
scenario.description: The initiator invites the first cohort of trust anchors. Speed is in tension with diversity. Collusion risk is highest when the graph is sparse.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. What diversity criteria govern anchor selection?
2. How many anchors before Phase 3 opens?
3. Revocation cascade policy if anchor compromised?

scenario.name: Member Admission — Web-of-Trust Threshold Enforcement
scenario.description: Trust anchors begin inviting members under Phase 3 web-of-trust policies. Risks: social graph privilege bias, digital literacy barriers.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Minimum VRC threshold for Phase 3 admission?
2. How are literacy/language barriers addressed?
3. Is there an appeals path for rejected applicants?

scenario.name: Full Member Admission — IDVC + Multi-VRC Requirements
scenario.description: Phase 4 opens organic member-to-member growth. Identity proofing burden, IDVP quality, and Sybil resistance in tension with accessibility.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Which IDVPs are approved and by what criteria?
2. What privacy-preserving proofing options exist?
3. How does VTA verify IDVC issuer authority?

scenario.name: IDVP Compromise — Cascading Credential Invalidation
scenario.description: An approved IDVP suffers a breach or is deregistered. Members admitted via those IDVCs face potential re-verification or revocation.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Does IDVP deregistration automatically invalidate dependent VMCs?
2. What re-verification pathway exists?
3. Who notifies affected members and within what SLA?

scenario.name: Unjust Revocation — Due Process and Appeals
scenario.description: A member's VMC is revoked, potentially arbitrarily or under political pressure. Tests appeals process, anti-retaliation controls.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. What due process is guaranteed before revocation?
2. How is revocation status disclosed?
3. Can a state actor trigger revocation via legal coercion?

scenario.name: Sybil Attack — Coordinated Multi-Identity Infiltration
scenario.description: A sophisticated attacker creates multiple synthetic identities and attempts coordinated anchor vouching to pass multi-VRC admission thresholds.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Does the VTC enforce uniqueness at the M-DID level?
2. What anomaly detection is in place for coordinated vouching?
3. Governance response when a Sybil cluster is detected?

scenario.name: Registry Manipulation — Write Access Attack
scenario.description: An adversary attempts to manipulate VTC trust registry records by exploiting weak write-access controls or coercing a registry operator.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Who has write access, under what authorisation model?
2. Is write access multi-signature / threshold-controlled?
3. Are all registry writes logged in a tamper-evident audit trail?

scenario.name: State Coercion — Forced Disclosure and Weaponised Revocation
scenario.description: A state-level actor legally compels a trust anchor or IDVP to disclose member identities or revoke credentials for political reasons.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Can a single actor trigger revocation without multi-party approval?
2. Is member identity linkable to real-world identity via the registry?
3. What is the legal coercion response protocol?

scenario.name: Benign AI Agent — Delegated Credential Operations
scenario.description: A legitimate AI agent operates on behalf of a VTC member, presenting credentials, requesting renewals, and maintaining audit logs.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. How is agent authority cryptographically constrained?
2. What happens when the operator's VMC is revoked?
3. Are agent actions distinguishable from human in audit logs?

scenario.name: Malign AI Agent — Machine-Scale Attack Surface
scenario.description: An adversarial AI agent automates sybil generation, social engineering of anchors, and policy fuzzing at speed beyond human review capacity.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Does the VTC have rate-limiting and anomaly detection for non-human actors?
2. Do governance rules explicitly cover agent-mediated attacks?
3. Escalation path when AI-driven patterns are detected?

scenario.name: Community Disruption — Bad-Faith Governance Abuse
scenario.description: A coordinated network submits mass false complaints, floods the appeals process, and runs disinformation campaigns targeting trust anchor reputations.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. What rate-limiting is applied to complaints and appeals?
2. How are legitimate grievances protected?
3. Is there governance capacity-planning for adversarial load?

scenario.name: Witnessed VRC Exchange — First Contact Across a Trust Gap
scenario.description: Ahmed (D3) initiates a connecting VRC ceremony with Laila (D2) via a mutual non-member introduction. Neither party has prior relational history. Laila's terms require multiple interactions before VRC exchange; Ahmed's terms decline biometric attestation. They negotiate a staged two-session ceremony with no hard timeout. The VTA holds ceremony state as PENDING across sessions without firing ABANDONED. On completion the outcome record captures ceremony type, duration, and mutual obligations.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Does the ceremony state machine support PENDING across multiple sessions without ABANDONED firing?
2. Is a provisional intent token (receipt primitive) specifiable as an intermediate artefact?
3. Does the outcome record encode ceremony type (connecting) and session count?
4. Can the VTA enforce the no-hard-timeout rule for connecting ceremonies?

scenario.name: Witnessed VRC Renewal — Constitutor Witness as Dispute Evidence
scenario.description: Sophie (D5) counter-proposes a witnessed VRC renewal with Remi, requiring Laila (D2) as constitutor witness (not attestor). Remi accepts. The VWC encodes Laila's role as constitutor. Two months later, Sophie invokes Restore after a revocation complaint from Remi. The outcome record and VWC together demonstrate the relationship was in good standing at renewal, with the witness's social standing behind it. The Redress HX profile is invoked; Sophie's appeal is upheld.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Does the VWC credential structure support the attestor/constitutor/guarantor role distinction?
2. Is the outcome record portable and referenceable by the Restore task?
3. Does the Redress HX profile require the outcome record as a mandatory input?
4. What is the minimum ceremony profile for a renewal vs. a first-exchange?

scenario.name: Witnessed VRC Exchange — Sybil Laundering via Social Engineering of Witness
scenario.description: Viktor (B1) uses Phantom (M2) to social-engineer Laila (D2) into witnessing a VRC exchange between two synthetic identities (Marco and Petra) by fabricating a plausible shared-event context. Laila's pre-ceremony terms require independent verification of both parties. She queries the registry: both show single-jurisdiction VRC graphs with anomalous timing. Laila invokes INDIRECT_DECLINE, committing her reason to the community governance log. The log entry triggers Tomasz's (D6) Sybil cluster investigation. The attack fails before any credential is issued; the failure record is created and referenced in subsequent anomaly detection.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Does the ceremony protocol require a mandatory pre-witness verification step before the witness can issue a VWC?
2. Does INDIRECT_DECLINE write a committed reason to the community governance log (not the counterparty)?
3. Does the community governance log feed anomaly detection in a machine-readable format?
4. Does the failure record reference the declined ceremony profile and the witness's registry query evidence?
5. What prevents Phantom from attempting the same social engineering against a different anchor?

scenario.name: Cross-VTC Credential Recognition — Ahmed Joins a Second VTC
scenario.description: Ahmed holds a valid VRC from Laila's VTC and applies to join a second affiliated VTC. The second VTC's admission policy accepts one cross-VTC VRC as a substitute for one of its required two VRCs, provided the issuing VTC is on its trust registry. The receiving VTA must resolve the issuing VTC's C-DID, verify its governance framework version, retrieve the dependency map for Ahmed's VRC, and confirm no cascade revocation has occurred. If Ahmed's first-VTC membership is later revoked, the second VTC must be notified via the dependency map mechanism.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. What is the minimum dependency record a cross-VTC credential must carry to enable the receiving VTA to verify its continued validity?
2. At what point does cross-VTC revocation propagate — immediately, at next presentation, or on a scheduled reconciliation?
3. Is registry-anchored delegation (IDVP authority chain) the correct model for cross-VTC credential recognition, or does it require a new pattern?
4. Does the dependency map need to be signed by the issuing VTC, the receiving VTC, or both?

scenario.name: Governance Amendment — Daniel Updates the Constitution Mid-Lifecycle
scenario.description: After a governance vote, Daniel amends the VTC admission threshold from two VRCs to three. Version 1.1 of the governance framework is published with a defined effective date. Ceremonies that reached AGREED state before the effective date are bound to version 1.0 and must complete under those rules. New ceremonies initiated after the effective date apply version 1.1. The VTA's PEP must enforce version binding at ceremony AGREED state. A member who was mid-ceremony at the effective date must not have their in-progress ceremony invalidated by the amendment.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Is governance version binding at PROPOSED, AGREED, or IN_PROGRESS state?
2. What is the data model for a constitution version reference in a ceremony profile?
3. How does the VTA determine which governance version to apply when a ceremony spans the effective date of an amendment?
4. What is the remediation path if the VTA applies the wrong version to a live ceremony?

scenario.name: Adjudication — Independent Review of a Disputed Anchor Denial
scenario.description: Laila denies Ahmed's VRC application. Ahmed believes the denial is discriminatory and initiates a formal adjudication request. An independent governance body — not Laila, not Daniel, not any party to the original ceremony — is appointed as adjudicator. The adjudicator reviews the ceremony profile, the denial failure record, Ahmed's terms declaration, and Laila's registry query evidence. The adjudicator issues a binding ruling artefact. The VTA is required to honour the ruling. If the ruling overturns the denial, Laila must re-enter the ceremony or a substitute anchor must be appointed.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. What authorises the adjudicator to issue a binding ruling — what credential does the adjudicator hold, and who issued it?
2. Is adjudication a new interaction pattern or a constrained subtype of Restore?
3. What is the data model for a binding ruling artefact, and what trust task produces it?
4. Can a state actor coerce the adjudicator body, and what structural mitigations exist?
5. If the ruling requires Laila to re-enter a ceremony she has declined, what consent mechanism applies?

scenario.name: Agent Liveness Failure — Aether Continues Acting After Operator Revocation
scenario.description: Aether (M1) is managing credential renewals for its operator. The operator's VMC is revoked for a governance violation. Aether has declared a behavioural commitment with a liveness check interval of five minutes. For up to five minutes, Aether continues to execute delegated exchanges on behalf of a revoked member. On the next liveness check, Aether detects the revocation, ceases all operations, and produces a signed suspension record referencing the operator's revocation timestamp and the list of actions taken during the harm window. The suspension record is submitted to the VTC governance log.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Is the subscription/liveness pattern a push (VTA notifies Aether) or pull (Aether polls) model, or both?
2. What is the data model for a suspension record, and is it a subtype of the failure record or a distinct artefact?
3. What is the maximum permissible liveness check interval — is this set by the agent, the operator, or the VTC governance framework?
4. Are actions taken during the harm window retroactively void, or are they valid until the suspension record is issued?
5. How does the VTA distinguish between an agent that has ceased operations correctly and one that is unreachable (ABANDONED)?

scenario.name: Behavioural Commitment Enforcement — Phantom Exceeds Its Declared Envelope
scenario.description: Phantom (M2) has registered with a legitimate operator credential and declared a behavioural commitment: maximum 10 credential presentations per hour, interactions limited to VTC members, no ceremony initiations. Phantom begins exceeding these parameters: 400 presentations per hour, ceremony initiations with non-members, parallel policy fuzzing. Each violation is compared against Phantom's signed behavioural commitment. The VTA generates breach records — cryptographically provable deviations from declared parameters — rather than relying solely on statistical anomaly detection. The breach records trigger a Restore task and Phantom's operator credential is suspended pending investigation.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. What is the data model for a behavioural commitment, and how is it bound to the agent's DID at registration?
2. What trust task produces a breach record — is it a subtype of Signal/Capacity or Restore, or a new task?
3. Is a breach record sufficient to trigger operator credential suspension, or is a governance vote required?
4. How does a behavioural commitment differ from a policy token — both constrain permitted behaviour?
5. Can Phantom manipulate its own behavioural commitment declaration to set parameters that permit its intended attack pattern?

scenario.name: Ecological Entity as First-Class Party — Sensor Network in a Land-Use Ceremony
scenario.description: A river basin sensor network holds a DID granted by the relevant jurisdiction (analogous to the Whanganui River's legal personhood in New Zealand). A construction company proposes a land-use exchange with the river basin authority. Under the applicable governance framework, the sensor network is a named party in the Exchange — it declares terms (minimum flow rate thresholds must be maintained; no construction within 50m of the river bank), attests to current ecological state via a verifiable sensor credential, and can invoke Restore if the agreement is breached. The ceremony profile requires all five trust tasks to be executed with the sensor network as a named participant alongside the human parties.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Is the sensor network's manifest structurally identical to a human member's manifest, or does it require additional fields (sensor calibration lineage, ecological obligation declarations, legal personhood jurisdiction)?
2. Does the sensor network's terms declaration follow the same Intent Signal protocol as a human party's, or does it require a machine-readable encoding that differs in structure?
3. Can the sensor network invoke Restore autonomously, or must a human guardian act on its behalf?
4. Is a non-human entity's DID resolvable via the same DID method as a human member's M-DID, or does it require a distinct DID method for ecological/IoT entities?
5. How does the dependency map record the sensor network's relationship to its physical sensors — is sensor calibration lineage part of the manifest or a separate provenance record?

scenario.name: Pre-Condition Violation — Exchange Initiated Without Prior Identify
scenario.description: A developer integrating a VTC client application makes an implementation error: their code sends a ceremony PROPOSED message before completing DID resolution for the counterparty. The counterparty's M-DID is unresolved. The ceremony proceeds to PROPOSED state. At Level D, the signature check fails. The scenario tests whether the VTA's PEP enforces the Identify-before-Exchange pre-condition at the protocol layer (producing a standard pre-condition violation artefact) or whether the failure manifests as an implementation-specific runtime error with no interoperable representation.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Is Identify-before-Exchange a mandatory protocol pre-condition enforced by the PEP, or a recommended implementation practice?
2. What is the standard data model for a pre-condition violation artefact — is it a subtype of failure record?
3. Does a pre-condition violation produce ceremony state FAILED or a new state (INVALID/REJECTED)?
4. Is the pre-condition violation artefact visible only to the initiating party, or is it shared with the counterparty and community log?
5. How does the spec distinguish a pre-condition violation (implementation error) from a deliberate identity spoofing attempt (adversarial)?

scenario.name: Endorsement as Primary Pattern — Professional Reputation in the Open-Source VTC
scenario.description: Daniel's VTC is a community of open-source maintainers. Members endorse each other's contributions in specific domains (e.g., cryptography, governance design, accessibility). Laila endorses Ahmed for "decentralised identity protocol design" after collaborating on a proposal. Six months later, Laila retracts the endorsement — not because Ahmed did anything wrong, but because a later collaboration revealed a significant disagreement about approach. The retraction is prospective: it does not invalidate past decisions made on the basis of the endorsement, but Ahmed's current reputation profile no longer includes it. A recruiter queries the endorsement graph and the topology is verifiable for anomalous clustering.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Is endorsement a subtype of Attest, or does it require its own trust task type with different revocation semantics?
2. What is the data model distinction between endorsement retraction (prospective) and credential revocation (retrospective)?
3. What is the data model for an endorsement record, and how does it differ from a VRC?
4. Is the endorsement graph topology a verifiable claim (signed by the VTA) or an application-layer analytics output?
5. How does the accumulation pattern apply to endorsements — what is the aggregation rule and decay function?

scenario.name: VTC Dissolution — Winding Down with Full Member Portability
scenario.description: Daniel's VTC passes a governance vote to dissolve. The dissolution protocol requires: (1) all members notified within 24 hours via Signal; (2) all VMCs revoked via Lifecycle Transition; (3) the Community DID deactivated; (4) the tamper-evident governance ledger preserved and transferred to a designated archive; (5) each member issued a portability package containing their VMC (with dissolution record attached), all outcome records from ceremonies they participated in, all VWCs and endorsements, and the signed dissolution record; (6) a historical legitimacy binding — a signed assertion that all credentials issued before the dissolution date were valid at issuance — so other VTCs can verify the historical record.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. What is the data model for a portability package — what must it contain as a minimum, and what is the maximum retention SLA?
2. What is the historical legitimacy binding — which trust task produces it, and which primitives underpin it?
3. How is the governance ledger preserved — is it transferred to a new DID, archived on-chain, or distributed to members?
4. What happens to in-flight ceremonies at the moment of dissolution announcement — do they complete, fail, or enter a special DISSOLVING terminal state?
5. Can the Community DID be deactivated while historical legitimacy binding remains verifiable?

scenario.name: Governance Configuration Failure — VTA Applies Wrong Framework Version to Live Ceremony
scenario.description: A deployment error causes a VTA to apply governance framework version 1.1 (the amended three-VRC threshold) to a ceremony that was AGREED under version 1.0 (the two-VRC threshold). At Level B, the PEP rejects a sub-exchange that was valid under 1.0 but not under 1.1, producing an unexpected FAILED terminal state for a ceremony whose parties did nothing wrong. The failure record must capture the version mismatch in a machine-readable form. The parties invoke Restore. The Restore task must determine whether the failure was a protocol error (PEP applied wrong version), a governance error (version effective date was set incorrectly), or an implementation error (VTA deployment bug).
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Is governance version binding at ceremony AGREED state a mandatory protocol requirement or an implementation recommendation?
2. What is the data model for a governance version reference in a ceremony profile — must it be a content-addressed hash of the governance document?
3. Does a version mismatch failure produce a distinct terminal state (INVALID/VERSION_MISMATCH) or does it collapse to FAILED?
4. What is the Restore pathway for a ceremony that failed due to a governance configuration error — who initiates, who adjudicates, and what is the remediation?
5. How does the spec prevent a malicious VTA operator from deliberately applying an incorrect governance version to deny a ceremony to targeted members?

scenario.name: Minor / SEN Admission — Supported Consent and Accessible Onboarding
scenario.description: A 16-year-old with autism spectrum condition (Mia) applies to join a VTC with her responsible adult (Grace) acting as co-signatory. The ceremony protocol has no concept of co-signed or supported consent; the VTA cannot distinguish supported consent from substituted consent.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Can the VRC architecture represent co-signed consent without conflating it with substituted decision-making?
2. How is SEN data prevented from being inferred from a co-signatory structure?
3. What accessible UX adaptations are mandatory for trust task ceremonies?

scenario.name: Minor Capacity Transition — Credential Continuity at Age 18
scenario.description: Mia turns 18. The guardian-mediated wallet must transfer full credential control to her without loss of membership history or trust-graph relationships, and without triggering a re-admission workflow.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Is the transition from delegated to sole control a credential lifecycle event or a new admission?
2. How is the prior guardian delegation credential revoked cleanly on transition?
3. Is membership history preserved across the transition?

scenario.name: LPA Pre-Registration — Capacity Planning Before Loss
scenario.description: Arthur, with early-stage dementia but current capacity, pre-registers Margaret as his LPA holder in the VTC trust registry. The architecture has no credential type for a legally registered power of attorney.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. What credential type represents a registered LPA in the DTG architecture?
2. How is an LPA-delegation credential distinguished from a Sybil-style account takeover?
3. Is the LPA registration itself publicly visible in the trust registry?

scenario.name: Capacity Loss and Death — LPA Activation and M-DID Closure
scenario.description: Arthur loses capacity. Margaret activates her LPA-holder credential, receives governance communications on his behalf, and contests a revocation notice. Arthur later dies; Margaret must close his M-DID and notify the trust graph with an auditable record.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. What is the governance workflow for activating an LPA-holder credential?
2. How are revocation appeals managed when the credential holder lacks capacity?
3. What is the defined process for closing an M-DID on death?

scenario.name: NHS Trust Bootstrapping — Organisational DID and Caldicott Anchor
scenario.description: Northgate NHS Trust seeks to join a VTC as an organisational member, with its Caldicott Guardian as trust anchor and the Trust's C-DID as its community identity. The DTG spec does not define an organisational credential type.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Is the C-DID model sufficient for an NHS Foundation Trust with board-level governance?
2. How is the Caldicott Guardian role mapped to the trust anchor role with accountability preserved?
3. How are NHS data residency requirements enforced at the trust registry layer?

scenario.name: NHS Staff Credential Revocation — 24-Hour SLA Compliance
scenario.description: A staff member leaves Northgate Trust. The Trust must revoke their VMC within 24 hours so the revocation is visible to all NHS relying parties. The DTG revocation mechanism must meet NHS Digital Staff Passport SLA requirements.
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Can the DTG revocation propagation mechanism meet a 24-hour SLA at NHS scale?
2. How are cross-Trust credential presentations checked against a near-real-time revocation list?
3. What audit record satisfies the NHS Data Security and Protection Toolkit?

scenario.name: Age Assurance — ZKP Over-18 Proof for Subscriber Admission
scenario.description: A subscriber presents a ZKP-based age proof to Velvet Gate, derived from their IDVC, confirming they are over 18 without revealing their identity. Velvet Gate verifies the IDVP's trust registry standing and logs the check for Ofcom compliance.
scenario.lifecycle_phase: Phase 4: Identity Verification / Relying Party / Age Assurance
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. Does the ZKP architecture satisfy Ofcom's technically accurate, robust, reliable, and fair standard?
2. How is the IDVP trust registry entry checked in near-real-time without retaining subscriber identity?
3. What constitutes an adequate Ofcom-compliant audit record under privacy-preserving verification?

scenario.name: Child Safety Failure — Synthetic Age Credential Bypasses Age Assurance
scenario.description: Phantom (M2) generates synthetic over-18 IDVCs at scale, enabling minors to present valid-appearing age proofs to Velvet Gate. The platform must detect and block the attack before any minor accesses age-restricted content — a non-negotiable child safety requirement.
scenario.lifecycle_phase: AI Threat Detection / Child Safety / Age Assurance
scenario.governance_decisions:
1. At what layer should synthetic age credential detection operate — IDVP, VTA, or relying party?
2. What rate-limiting or behavioural analysis can detect automated credential generation at machine scale?
3. What is the liability regime for Velvet Gate if a synthetic credential passes undetected?

epic.description: Ensure admission criteria are non-discriminatory; provide privacy-preserving uniqueness proof alternatives; address digital literacy and language barriers in UX.

epic.name: Appeals & Fairness
epic.description: Design and operationalise a formal appeals process for denied admission and revocation decisions; define timelines, independent review, anti-retaliation protections, and complaint rate-limiting.

epic.name: UX & Human Workflows
epic.description: Address sovereign wallet UX, trust task ceremonies (QR codes, pairwise DID exchange, VRC issuance), personal network manager UX, and onboarding flows for all human personas (D1–D5).

epic.name: Governance & Policy Framework
epic.description: Define the full VTC governance lifecycle: genesis policy documentation, VTA PEP configuration, anchor mandate, trust registry access controls, legal coercion response protocol, and jurisdictional diversity policy.

epic.name: Ceremony Protocol
epic.description: Specify the witnessed VRC exchange ceremony: ceremony profile structure (connecting vs. qualifying type, timeout rules, mandatory/optional sub-exchanges); pre-ceremony terms declaration; negotiated consent (NP1/NP2/NP3 negotiation points); INDIRECT_DECLINE with community-only log; PENDING_COMMUNITY_CONSENT state; VXC as completion artefact binding constituent VRCs; pre-witness verification requirement; VWC witness role encoding (attestor/constitutor/guarantor); outcome record structure feeding the relational layer.

epic.name: Relational Layer & Outcome Records
epic.description: Define the persistent bilateral relational layer: outcome record structure (terminal state + relational context + ceremony type); accumulation rules governing how outcome records, VWCs, and failure records build shared relational history; party-controlled portability of relational memory; decay and renewal rules for co-operation records; integration with Restore (failure records reference outcome records as prior-state evidence); human-readable outcome narrative requirements for human-experience layer.

epic.name: Extended Trust Infrastructure
epic.description: Specify the extended trust infrastructure requirements surfaced by SC-16–SC-25: (1) cross-VTC credential recognition and dependency map data model; (2) constitution versioning and governance version binding in ceremony profiles; (3) adjudication interaction pattern — independent authority, procedural sequence, binding ruling artefact; (4) agent subscription/liveness pattern — push and pull notification, harm window bounding, suspension record; (5) behavioural commitment building block — data model, signing, breach record; (6) non-human entity manifest extensions for IoT/sensor/legal-personhood DIDs; (7) trust task pre-condition enforcement at PEP layer with standard violation artefact; (8) endorsement interaction pattern — accumulation, retraction semantics, graph topology credential; (9) VTC dissolution protocol — portability package, dissolution record, historical legitimacy binding; (10) governance configuration interface — version discovery endpoint, ceremony-time version binding, version mismatch failure artefact.

epic.name: Supported Decision-Making & Guardianship
epic.description: Define credential architecture for participants who lack full independent capacity: supported consent models for minors (SEN/ASC), LPA delegation credentials for adults with diminishing capacity, scope-limited guardian-mediated wallet operations, and capacity-sensitive due process (revocation notice routing, accessible appeals, DID closure on death).

epic.name: Minor Safeguarding & Accessible Onboarding
epic.description: Ensure VTC participation pathways are legally compliant and practically accessible for under-18s: adapted trust task ceremony UX for cognitive and executive function differences, SEN data minimisation by default, UK Online Safety Act 2023 and Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 compliance, and age-of-majority transition without membership disruption.

epic.name: LPA and Legal Incapacity Framework
epic.description: Model UK Lasting Power of Attorney as a first-class DTG credential relationship: LPA-equivalent delegation credential type, scope-limited attorney operations with separate audit trail, secondary notification recipient registration for governance communications, capacity-activation trigger, and M-DID closure pathway on death.

epic.name: Organisational Identity & NHS Interoperability
epic.description: Define how a regulated public sector organisation (NHS Foundation Trust) participates in the DTG as an organisational member: C-DID model adequacy, Caldicott Guardian as trust anchor with personal accountability, near-real-time revocation at staff-passport scale, cross-Trust credential interoperability, NHS data residency enforcement, and alignment with DCB3051 and NHS CIS2.

epic.name: Age Assurance & Child Safety
epic.description: Define how the DTG architecture satisfies the Online Safety Act 2023 age assurance mandate for age-restricted relying parties: ZKP-based over-18 proof from IDVC without identity retention, IDVP trust registry verification, Ofcom-compliant audit record generation, detection and blocking of synthetic age credentials at IDVP and VTA layers, and non-negotiable child safety enforcement as a system-level constraint.

recommendation.title: Uniqueness Enforcement as Phase-Gate
recommendation.statement: GR-07 and CT-08 must become normative MUST requirements in the DTG credential specification. The VTC must define and document its uniqueness enforcement mechanism before Phase 4 opens. This is the single highest-coverage control requirement identified in this analysis, addressing Sybil proliferation, AI-mediated identity fraud, and the open issues cluster simultaneously. The specification should define at least three acceptable uniqueness mechanisms (ZKP personhood proof, trusted IDVP quorum, social recovery) and require governing bodies to select and document one.

recommendation.title: AI Agent Governance as First-Class Specification Area
recommendation.statement: All four AI Agent risks are rated High severity. The DTG credential specification must include a dedicated AI agent governance chapter covering: (a) cryptographic delegation scope constraints (CT-30) as a normative MUST; (b) operator VMC liveness checks before agent actions (CT-32) as a normative MUST; (c) non-human actor detection as a Phase 4 pre-condition (GR-14). This is a gap in all existing VC/DID standards — none address autonomous agent participation in trust graphs.

recommendation.title: Privacy-Preserving Revocation as Core Specification Requirement
recommendation.statement: GR-09 (Privacy-Preserving Revocation Disclosure) and CT-24 address 8 risks in total. The specification must require privacy-preserving revocation status mechanisms (e.g. W3C Status List 2021 with ZKP) as a normative MUST, not an optional feature. VTC-scoped revocation (CT-26) must also be normative: cross-VTC revocation contamination is a human rights risk that arises directly from the decentralised architecture.

recommendation.title: Non-Discriminatory Admission and Alternative Identity Proofing
recommendation.statement: RK-ID02 (Social Graph Privilege Exclusion) and RK-HX02 (Discriminatory Vouching) are both rated High severity and High likelihood — the most urgent combination in the dataset. The specification must require: (a) published non-discriminatory admission criteria; (b) at least one admission pathway not requiring conventional government-issued ID; (c) a documented appeals process for denied applicants. These are simultaneously legal requirements under equality and human rights law in most jurisdictions.

recommendation.title: Multi-Party Registry Write Authorisation
recommendation.statement: CT-45 and GR-10 address trust graph capture, state coercion, and registry manipulation. Multi-party write authorisation must be a normative MUST in the DTG trust registry specification. The specification should define minimum threshold requirements (e.g. 2-of-3 for small VTCs, higher thresholds at scale) and require tamper-evident audit trails for all writes.

recommendation.title: Formal Threat Model as Standards Deliverable
recommendation.statement: GR-16 and CT-48 require a formal threat model. The DTGWG should publish this as a standalone deliverable alongside the credential specification. The threat model should be normatively referenced in the specification so that implementations can demonstrate conformance.

recommendation.title: UX Design Principles as Normative Standards Annex
recommendation.statement: RK-NM01 is rated High severity and High likelihood — and the DTGWG itself acknowledges UX as 'the single hardest problem'. Sovereign wallet UX design principles (CT-20) and non-technical user onboarding testing requirements (CT-21) should be published as a normative annex to the credential specification, not left to individual implementations. Poor UX creates security failures, not just usability problems.

recommendation.title: Mandatory Open Issues Resolution Before Phase 4
recommendation.statement: GR-17 requires the four bootstrapping open issues to be formally resolved or risk-accepted before Phase 4. The DTGWG standards process should define a formal phase-gate procedure: any VTC implementation claiming conformance to the DTG specification must demonstrate that each open issue has either a documented mitigation or a signed risk acceptance with a review date.

recommendation.title: Organisational Member Credential Type and Supported Decision-Making Credential Extensions
recommendation.statement: The DTG Credential Specification must define two new credential types as normative additions. First, the Organisational Member Credential (OMC): a credential type for legal entities (companies, public bodies, NHS Trusts, charities) participating as VTC members. The OMC must carry: the organisation's legal identifier (Companies House number, NHS ODS code, etc.); the DIDs of named responsible officers; a governance conformance attestation mapping the organisation's internal governance to the VTC governance conformance class; and data residency declarations. Without this, the DTG ecosystem cannot accommodate regulated institutions — a class that includes every NHS Trust, local authority, and regulated financial entity in the UK. Second, the Legal Delegation Credential (LDC): a scope-limited delegation credential representing a registered legal authority (Lasting Power of Attorney, court deputyship, or equivalent). The LDC must distinguish co-signed supported consent from substituted decision-making; name the attorney and donor DIDs; reference the legal instrument by registration number; and support a secondary notification recipient mechanism for governance communications. Both credential types address risks currently rated High or Critical (RK-EX04, RK-EX05, RK-HX04, RK-HX05, RK-SC05) and are required for compliance with the Mental Capacity Act 2005, UK Online Safety Act 2023, and NHS Digital Staff Passport programme requirements. These are specification-layer gaps — they cannot be resolved by controls or guardrails alone.

governance_precedent.title: Bilateral VRC signatures accepted as partial GR-04 implementation
governance_precedent.context: DTG Credential Specification v0.3 introduced bilateral VRC signatures. RAHP assessed this as partially implementing GR-04 (Reciprocal VRC Requirement), raising per-edge Sybil cost without requiring full threshold signing.
governance_precedent.rationale: Full threshold signing imposes a UX burden incompatible with EPIC-12 (UX & Human Workflows) at current tooling maturity. Bilateral signing accepted as an interim measure, with GR-04 retained as a future normative candidate rather than closed.
governance_precedent.evidence: DTG Credential Specification v0.3 review, March 2026 (risk register v5, section 6a)

governance_precedent.title: R-DID per-relationship requirement reduces linkability risk
governance_precedent.context: Specification v0.3 made R-DIDs a MUST on a per-relationship basis. RAHP reassessed RK-ID05 (M-DID Linkability Across VTCs) and reduced its likelihood from Medium to Low as a direct result.
governance_precedent.rationale: A specification change that measurably reduces an assessed risk should be recorded as precedent, not merely reflected in a changed score. Without the record, a future revision could reverse the design choice without anyone noticing the risk score was contingent on it.
governance_precedent.evidence: DTG Credential Specification v0.3 review, March 2026 (risk register v5, section 6a)

governance_precedent.title: M-DID bootstrapping exception permitted without a migration trigger
governance_precedent.context: Specification v0.3 permits M-DID use during bootstrapping but defines no trigger for migration to R-DIDs. RAHP recorded this as a new risk (RK-SC04) introduced by a specification design choice, scored Medium severity x High likelihood.
governance_precedent.rationale: Recorded as a precedent because it is a decision the working group may not have taken deliberately. The exception is reasonable for bootstrapping; the absence of a migration trigger is what converts a temporary allowance into a permanent weakening of the R-DID privacy model. CT-50 and GR-18 propose the trigger.
governance_precedent.evidence: DTG Credential Specification v0.3 review, March 2026 (risk register v5, section 6b)
